articles.title: Damian Lillard Explains Process Behind Achieving 100K Shots Goal in New Video Amid Injury Rehab
articles.summary: Portland Trail Blazers star Damian Lillard explained what led to his goal of making 100,000 shots while missing the entire 2025-26 season as he recovered from a torn Achilles.
articles.body:
Portland Trail Blazers star Damian Lillard explained what led to his goal of making 100,000 shots while missing the entire 2025-26 season as he recovered from a torn Achilles .

Lillard revealed that the process started after he was putting up shots that were tracked by Portland's staff once he was cleared to resume basketball activities.

"Eventually once I got to about 8,000 I was like 'By this time next year, I'm gonna try to make 100,000,'" Lillard said in a video posted by the Trail Blazers on X (0:25 mark). "Then we really started tracking every workout that I did. We made sure that those numbers went into the system. Today was the day that I was able to cross over that 100,000 mark."

The nine-time All-Star previously revealed that he reached his goal, which started in Sept. 2025, in a post on his Instagram Story .

Lillard has already established himself as one of the greatest long-range shooters in NBA history, as he sits at No. 5 on the league's all-time three-point shooting leaderboard .

He remained active despite being sidelined last season, as he still ended up winning the 3-Point Contest during the 2026 All-Star festivitiues.

Lillard will now look to return during his 2026-27 campaign and provide a boost to a Trail Blazers squad that ended a four-year playoff drought last season.

articles.title: Biggest Winners and Losers from NBA's Ruling on LA Clippers, Kawhi Leonard
articles.summary: On September 3, 2025, Pablo Torre released his first podcast episode on Kawhi Leonard's no-show deal with the disgraced "green banking" company Aspiration.
articles.body:
On September 3, 2025, Pablo Torre released his first podcast episode on Kawhi Leonard's no-show deal with the disgraced "green banking" company Aspiration.

One day before the anniversary of that episode, the NBA has dropped the proverbial hammer on the team it says helped facilitate deals that ultimately amounted to cap circumvention.

ESPN's Shams Charania summarized the punishments on X.

Now, it's time to sort through the fines, pick forfeitures and suspensions and assign the biggest names involved to either side of the "winners and losers" ledger.

There are some pretty obvious breaking news items that make it easy to list Los Angeles Clippers owner Steve Ballmer among today's losers.

The $30 million fine, practically speaking, won't hurt his pocketbook too much. It's less than half of one percent of his net worth, but there's certainly some reputational damage there.

For Ballmer, the one-year suspension is likely more painful. Few owners across sports are as passionate about their teams. Not being able to cheer his Clippers on in person is a real punishment.

But the biggest factor in Ballmer being here stems all the way back to last year, when shortly after Torre's first investigative report surfaced, he so aggressively denied any wrongdoing.

There can be some value in quickly reacting to a story like this and confidently refuting it, but you'd better have some foundation or evidence underneath that confidence. Without that, definitive statements can come back to haunt you.

Clearly, Ballmer wasn't speaking on the kind of steady ground he thought he had. And that very seriously calls his credibility into question.

Kawhi was the player at the center of this whole controversy. He received 10s of millions in impermissible benefits. And in the end, his contract wasn't voided, he wasn't suspended and he only had to pay $700,000 in restitution.

For a player with over $400 million in legal , on-the-court earnings, who also received $28 million from Aspiration (plus $20 million in stock options), and who gets to leave this mess behind and join the Toronto Raptors, that amounts to less than a slap on the wrist.

With five first-round picks surrendered and key front office personnel suspended, L.A. has truly been crippled by the Kawhi era. He simply gets to play next season with a new team (assuming his trade there is finally finalized), as though nothing happened.

There's at least a chance that he was sort of a patsy in all this. The punishments for the Clippers and the five-year ban for his uncle, Dennis Robertson, suggest that may be the case. But Kawhi had to know something was amiss when this company was paying as much as it did to literally do nothing. The NBA must not have had the foundation it needed to prove that.

Seven years ago, Clippers fans were exuberant over an offseason that saw them add reigning Finals MVP Kawhi and Paul George. Both superstars were in their primes, and it looked like they'd help L.A. compete for titles for years to come.

Now, in 2026, both are gone. The team only won three playoff series in the years since landing its star duo. And now, it has to forfeit at least one first-round pick in each of the 2029, 2030, 2031, 2032 and 2033 drafts.

Those assets being gone not only impact the team's long-term prospects but also make it harder to pull off win-now trades.

Assuming these punishments are upheld in Court (where the Clippers have vowed to take this matter), L.A. fans could be headed into an era packed with losing and with little more than memories of underachievement left to them by Kawhi.

In the wake of Wednesday's news, the Clippers released a statement that included the following:

"We intend to vigorously challenge these findings and penalties through every avenue available to us and look forward to an ethical and impartial arbitration process."

Charania later reported that arbitration isn't on the table, but L.A. could bring this before a Judge in court. And if that avenue overturns the penalties the NBA just announced, Adam Silver and the league could have a lot of egg to wipe off their faces.

But for now, it's only fair to give Silver, a commissioner who's taken plenty of understandable criticism in recent years, some flowers.

Based on nothing more than the publicly available reporting from Torre, there was no reasonable explanation for Kawhi's deals outside of cap circumvention. But that didn't necessarily mean Silver would hand down severe punishments.

Ballmer is the league's richest individual owner. That carries a lot of weight. Silver has long seemed reluctant to do anything that might jeopardize his standing with the players. These moves opened up the potential for conflict on both fronts. It took some courage to do that.

In the immediate aftermath of this news going public, it felt like this story finally had a resolution. And for fans who care about the integrity of the NBA and professional basketball generally, the resolution made sense.

But within an hour, we were reminded that this fight could drag on for months (or even years) through litigation. The saga may be far from over.

And if this becomes a very ugly, very public catfight between the league and its wealthiest owner, it's the fans who might suffer.

In the last few years, the NBA has had to ban a player (Jontay Porter) for life for fixing prop bets. It had an active head coach indicted for alleged participation in rigged poker games. It had other former and current players (including Terry Rozier) indicted for other betting schemes.

Each story on its own might be easy to survive. Stacked on top of each other, it starts to make it hard for NBA fans to trust the league.

For however long Silver remains the commissioner of the NBA, he needs to fight tooth and nail to restore some of the credibility it may have lost. Wednesday's news suggests he may be ready for that fight.

articles.title: Kawhi Leonard: Los Angeles Clippers fined $30m and stripped of five first-round picks after Leonard salary cap scandal
articles.summary: Los Angeles Clipper owner Steve Ballmer suspended for one year; team docked five first-round picks following NBA investigation into Kawhi Leonard salary cap scandal; The Clippers had said multiple times they had done nothing wrong and expected to be exonerated
articles.body:
The NBA came down hard on the organisation after a nearly year-long investigation with several additonal punishments given out, including:

Owner Steve Ballmer suspended for one year

President of basketball operations Lawrence Frank suspended without pay for six months

President of business operations Gillian Zucker suspended for one year

Clippers were also stripped of five first-round draft picks

The Clippers had said multiple times that they had done nothing wrong and expected to be exonerated.

"I accept full responsibility for lapses in judgment by people within my inner circle and regret the distraction this situation has caused the fans and my family," Leonard said in a statement issued through his new agent, Harrison Gaines.

The NBA said Leonard, through his former business manager and uncle Dennis Robertson, "violated the circumvention rules by pressuring the Clippers to assist him in obtaining off-court income opportunities, successfully obtaining those opportunities, and failing to reimburse payments by the Clippers for personal expenses."

Leonard added: "I entered into my contract with the Clippers as well as the agreements in question in good faith, fully committed to fulfilling my obligations and with no knowledge of any intent on anyone's part to circumvent the salary cap."

The league said Ballmer was suspended for "knowingly seeking to help Mr Leonard obtain off-court income opportunities," among other issues.

An investigation conducted by New York law firm Wachtell Lipton said the Clippers broke NBA rules by initiating off-court income opportunities between Leonard and four companies doing business with the team, as well as facilitating endorsement agreements between Leonard and the companies.

It added the Clippers "induced the companies to enter into these agreements by offering them business from the team", as well as paying personal expenses on behalf of Leonard and "failing to report improper solicitations for off-court income opportunities" made on Leonard's behalf through his then-business manager Dennis Robertson.

NBA Commissioner Adam Silver said: "The NBA's collectively bargained system for determining player compensation is a fundamental component of the basketball competition that the league oversees for the benefit of the teams and players and ultimately the fans. I am deeply disappointed by the flagrant violations of our rules and by the Clippers' institutional and leadership failures that led to this misconduct. The severity of the penalties reflects the seriousness of the violations."

Leonard, a two-time NBA champion and two-time Defensive Player of the Year, was subject to a trade agreement earlier this summer that was set to see him return to the Toronto Raptors. The deal was subsequently put on hold until the end of the NBA's investigation.

Who are the individuals involved in the scandal?

The report by Watchell, Lipton, Rosen and Katz identified Clippers owner Steve Ballmer , Clippers president of business operations Gillian Zucker and president of basketball operations Lawrence Frank as the three individuals most responsible for the Clippers' rule-breaking.

It detailed how Ballmer "knowingly sought to help Mr Leonard obtain off-court income opportunities" and how Zucker served as the point person on all four deals between the companies and the Clippers.

Frank, the primary team contact for Leonard's uncle and business manager Robertson, was found responsible for approving payments made by the Clippers for impermissible expenses incurred by Mr Leonard and his family.

articles.title: New Kawhi Leonard Rumors on Clippers-Raptors Trade After NBA Concludes Investigation
articles.summary: The blockbuster trade between the Los Angeles Clippers and Toronto Raptors involving Kawhi Leonard can move forward after the NBA concluded its investigation into the Clippers, according to ESPN's Shams Charania.
articles.body:
The blockbuster trade between the Los Angeles Clippers and Toronto Raptors involving Kawhi Leonard can move forward after the NBA concluded its investigation into the Clippers, according to ESPN's Shams Charania.

"There's full expectation that this trade will be going down as is between the Clippers and the Raptors that had multiple first-round picks, other swaps and second-round pick considerations going to the Clippers," Charania reported during a Wednesday appearance on SportsCenter (3:00 mark). "The trade is on track and both sides can now move forward with getting this deal done."

On Wednesday, the NBA announced that the Clippers and Leonard were both penalized for violating the salary cap circumvention rules contained in the collective bargaining agreement.

Toronto initially agreed to acquire Leonard in a trade with Los Angeles on June 30, although the swap was later put on hold due to the NBA's ongoing investigation.

The Raptors sent Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick, two future first-round picks, two second-round picks and one first-round pick swap to the Clippers in exchange for Leonard as part of the agreement.

Leonard previously spent one year with Toronto during the 2018-19 season, helping lead the team to a championship while earning Finals MVP honors.

He eventually joined Los Angeles during the 2019 offseason.

As part of the penalties announced by the NBA on Wednesday, the Clippers were fined $30 million and required to forfeit five first-round picks in 2029, 2030, 2031, 2032 and 2033.

Clippers governor Steve Ballmer was suspended from all league and team activities for one year due to his involvement, while president of basketball operations Lawrence Frank received a six-month suspension.

The Clippers released a statement in which they rejected the NBA's findings, although Charania noted that the league's rulings are final and there is no formal appeal or arbitration process. The organization's only avenue to fight the penalties is in court.

As for the Raptors, they're looking to contend in the Eastern Conference with Leonard after finishing with a 46-36 record and making a first-round playoff appearance last season.

The seven-time All-Star is joining a Toronto starting lineup that includes Scottie Barnes, RJ Barrett and Immanuel Quickley.

articles.title: Josh Hart Responds to Viral Post Debating if Knicks Won Mikal Bridges Blockbuster Trade with Nets
articles.summary: Josh Hart has declared the winner of the trade that sent Mikal Bridges from the Brooklyn Nets to the New York Knicks.
articles.body:
Josh Hart has declared the winner of the trade that sent Mikal Bridges from the Brooklyn Nets to the New York Knicks.

Responding to a post questioning who won the deal, Hart responded, "The team with the ring."

The Knicks gave up a lofty haul for Bridges, including four unprotected first-round picks. Many fans, including Knicks fans, questioned whether the swingman was worth that kind of package.

While he's had his ups and downs since joining New York, he was undoubtedly key to the team winning a championship. The Nets, meanwhile, went 26-56 in their first year without Bridges and went 20-62 last season.

The first-rounders should help the Nets as they continue their rebuild, but for now, it's more than fair to say that the Knicks are the winners of the trade.

articles.title: Ukrainian Center Koval Says She Left LSU Because Team Brought in Russian Player
articles.summary: BATON ROUGE, La. (AP) — Kate Koval says she decided to leave LSU because it brought in a Russian player, and the Ukrainian center is hoping the NCAA will permit her to play elsewhere this season.
articles.body:
BATON ROUGE, La. (AP) — Kate Koval says she decided to leave LSU because it brought in a Russian player, and the Ukrainian center is hoping the NCAA will permit her to play elsewhere this season.

Koval issued a statement on Instagram on Wednesday, just over a week after LSU coach Kim Mulkey announced the post player's departure.

"My father serves in the Ukrainian military and takes tremendous pride in defending his country against Russian aggression," Koval said. "For me, this war is not distant or abstract. People close to me have been killed and wounded in Russian attacks, and places where I grew up and first began playing basketball have been destroyed by missile strikes."

Mulkey had indicated Koval was leaving for personal reasons and that the program would respect her privacy regarding her decision.

LSU recently signed Anna Minaeva, a 6-foot-5 post player who previously played professionally with MBA Moscow.

Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and the two countries have been at war since.

"The timing of this situation and the deeply personal effect it has had on me, my family and those we care about who continue to live through and fight this war ultimately made me question whether LSU remained the right place for me," Koval said. "This decision has not been easy. While I understand and respect that roster decisions are a part of college basketball, I have to remain true to myself, my values and my country."

Koval averaged 8.3 points, 6.3 rebounds, 1.2 blocks and 16.6 minutes in 35 games for LSU last season. The 6-5 center played at Notre Dame in 2024-25 and averaged 5.3 points, 4.7 rebounds, 1.3 assists, 1.7 blocks and 18.3 minutes in 32 games.

In her statement, Koval noted that she didn't learn about LSU's decision to sign Minaeva until after the transfer portal had already closed.

"I hope the NCAA recognizes the circumstances surrounding my situation and understands the seriousness and deep nature of this matter," Koval said. "More than anything, I hope I am given the opportunity to compete at another school during the upcoming 2026-27 basketball season."

articles.title: NBA strips Clippers of 5 first-round draft picks after probe, fines Kawhi Leonard and Steve Ballmer
articles.summary: The NBA announced findings and penalties in connection with a yearlong investigation of the Clippers and Kawhi Leonard.
articles.body:
The NBA on Wednesday announced severe punishments for the Clippers -- including the loss of five future first-round picks and a fine of $30 million -- for violating salary cap circumvention rules when they signed star Kawhi Leonard in 2022.

In a statement, the NBA said a near-yearlong investigation "found a pattern of misconduct and multiple significant rules violations by the Clippers organization, a prior offender of the salary cap circumvention rules."

The punishments, as announced by the league, include:

The forfeiture of five first-round draft picks, one each in the 2029, 2030, 2031, 2032 and 2033 NBA drafts.

• Owner Steve Ballmer is suspended from all league and team activities for one year.

• President of business operations Gillian Zucker is suspended without pay for one year.

• President of basketball operations Lawrence Frank is suspended without pay for six months.

All penalties are binding, the league and the players' union said.

"The NBA's collectively bargained system for determining player compensation is a fundamental component of the basketball competition that the league oversees for the benefit of the teams and players and ultimately the fans," NBA commissioner Adam Silver said. "I am deeply disappointed by the flagrant violations of our rules and by the Clippers' institutional and leadership failures that led to this misconduct. The severity of the penalties reflects the seriousness of the violations."

Leonard, through his new agent, Harrison Gaines, said he accepted "full responsibility for lapses in judgment by people within my inner circle and regret the distraction this situation has caused the fans and my family."

"I entered into my contract with the Clippers as well as the agreements in question in good faith, fully committed to fulfilling my obligations and with no knowledge of any intent on anyone's part to circumvent the salary cap," he said.

The Clippers-Toronto Raptors agreed to a trade centered around Leonard earlier this summer, but that was put on hold until the NBA investigation was completed.

The investigation was conducted by New York law firm Wachtell Lipton, which released a summary report Wednesday.

It came after initial allegations that the Clippers compensated Leonard through a $28 million endorsement deal that he signed in 2022 with the now-bankrupt green banking company Aspiration, which also had a 23-year, $300 million endorsement deal with the Clippers. Those allegations were reported on initially by former ESPN contributor Pablo Torre in a series of podcasts last September.

The Wachtell Lipton investigation found that the Clippers broke rules by "initiating off-court income opportunities between Mr. Leonard and four companies doing business with the team: Aspiration Partners, Boingo Wireless, Daktronics, and Lockton Insurance; facilitating endorsement agreements between these companies and Mr. Leonard; inducing the companies to enter into these agreements by offering them business from the team; paying personal expenses on behalf of Mr. Leonard and his representatives; and failing to report improper solicitations for off-court income opportunities made on Mr. Leonard's behalf through his then-business manager, Dennis Robertson."

The Clippers said they intend to challenge the findings of the investigation "through every avenue available to us," while looking "forward to an ethical and impartial arbitration process."

Clippers owner Steve Ballmer denied any team involvement in the reported $28 million deal between star player Kawhi Leonard and the company Aspiration.

"We vehemently reject the NBA's findings, which are the result of a heavily biased investigation seeking to justify a predetermined narrative rather than facts and evidence," the team said in a statement. "What the league told us privately differs from what it announced today publicly, and they have not held themselves close to the standard Commissioner Silver set at the start of this investigation to ensure it's fairness and accuracy.

"For the past year, we cooperated fully and in good faith and we will now fight just as hard to demonstrate our innocence."

articles.title: Raptors Star Kawhi Leonard Breaks Silence After NBA Ruling
articles.summary: Kawhi Leonard addressed the NBA’s ruling and his return to Toronto, saying he wants to move forward with a “clean slate.” The post Raptors Star Kawhi Leonard...
articles.body:
Kawhi Leonard's return to Toronto has spent the summer trapped between nostalgia and an NBA investigation. On Wednesday, the biggest obstacle finally moved out of the way.

The NBA announced that Leonard and the Los Angeles Clippers violated the league's salary-cap circumvention rules, ending the central phase of an investigation that had prevented Toronto from completing its blockbuster trade for the two-time Finals MVP. Leonard was ordered to pay $700,000, while the Clippers received dramatically harsher penalties, including a $30 million fine and the forfeiture of five first-round picks.

Hours later, Leonard addressed the ruling — and his impending return to the Raptors — in a statement posted to Instagram.

"Integrity and respect for this game are fundamental to who I am," Leonard wrote. "I accept full responsibility for lapses in judgment by people within my inner circle and regret the distraction this situation has caused the fans and my family."

Leonard maintained that he entered his Clippers contract and the outside agreements "in good faith" and said he had no knowledge of an attempt to circumvent the salary cap.

Then came the line that will matter most in Toronto.

"As I return to Toronto, I am focused on what I can control, closing this chapter, and moving forward with a clean slate," Leonard wrote.

NBA Finds Clippers, Leonard Violated Salary-Cap Rules

The league's conclusions were far more severe than the relatively modest financial penalty imposed on Leonard.

According to the NBA, the Clippers created and facilitated off-court income opportunities for Leonard involving four companies that did business with the franchise: Aspiration Partners, Boingo Wireless, Daktronics and Lockton Insurance. The investigation also found that the Clippers paid personal expenses for Leonard and his representatives.

The league said Leonard, through former business manager Dennis Robertson, violated circumvention rules by pressuring the Clippers to help secure outside income opportunities and by failing to reimburse certain personal expenses. Robertson was banned from doing business with NBA teams for five years.

Clippers owner Steve Ballmer was suspended for one year. President of basketball operations Lawrence Frank received a six-month suspension, while business operations president Gillian Zucker was suspended for one year.

Commissioner Adam Silver called the violations "flagrant" and said the penalties reflected the seriousness of the misconduct.

Kawhi Leonard's Raptors Return Moves Forward

For the Toronto Taptors, the significance is more immediate.

The Raptors and Clippers agreed on June 30 to a deal sending Leonard back to Toronto for Brandon Ingram , Gradey Dick , unprotected first-round picks in 2031 and 2033, second-rounders in 2030 and 2033, and a 2027 first-round swap.

Toronto later put the transaction on hold after the NBA warned that the Raptors would assume the risk of any punishment attached to Leonard while the investigation remained unresolved. The Raptors publicly said they would wait for the probe to conclude.

articles.title: How hard did the NBA hit the Clippers? Here's how other recent cheating scandals have been handled
articles.summary: The Clippers don't control a first-round pick until 2034.
articles.body:
And what a hammer it was. The league has stripped the Clippers of five first-round draft picks, fined owner Steve Ballmer $30 million, fined Leonard $700,000 and suspended Ballmer, president of basketball operations Lawrence Frank and president of business operations Gillian Zucker.

It is a team-changing blow to LA, which many have noted also gave up five first-rounders, two pick swaps and future MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander in a trade for Paul George at Leonard's request.

The Clippers have already released a statement rejecting the NBA's findings and promising to challenge them . It remains to be seen how that will play out, but the NBA has certainly thrown down a harsh first move.

But how harsh is it compared to other cheating scandals in recent sports history? Let's compare the Clippers' sanctions to the bites other teams have received for bending the rules for a competitive advantage in recent sports history, which we are cutting off at the year 2000.

Note: This is purely a comparison of penalties for team cheating scandals. We will not be including any stories involving actual crimes (e.g. the Penn State scandal) nor cases of individual athletes being punished (e.g. Lance Armstrong).

The scandal: Former Astros pitcher Mike Fiers blew the whistle on the 2017 World Series champions using a live camera feed and a trash can to relay pitch signals to batters in real time. An MLB investigation followed, in which Astros players were offered immunity in exchange for honesty and confirmed the depth of the scheme, which included cheating in the Fall Classic.

The penalty: The Astros were fined $5 million, the maximum allowed by MLB and stripped of the first- and second-round picks in the 2020 and 2021 MLB drafts. General manager Jeff Luhnow, manager A.J. Hinch and 2017 bench coach Alex Cora were all suspended a full season. Carlos Beltran, one of the ringleaders of the scheme, also left his new job as manager of the New York Mets in the aftermath.

The Astros were allowed to keep the 2017 title, which remains one of the more tainted achievements in sports history.

The scandal : With in-person advance scouting against NCAA rules, Michigan staffer Connor Stalions devised a scheme where people would attend the games of future Michigan opponents in an attempt to decipher their signals. Stalions — who was even on the Central Michigan sideline in CMU gear in 2023 when the Chippewas played Michigan State — booked tickets to numerous teams that Michigan did and could play across multiple seasons. When the Big Ten's investigation into Stalions' scheme became public in October of 2023, then-Michigan coach Jim Harbaugh denied that he knew what was happening and said he had not "directed any staff member or others to participate in an off-campus scouting assignment."

The penalty : Less than two weeks after Stalions was suspended, he parted ways with Michigan. Harbaugh was suspended for the final three games of the 2023 regular season by the Big Ten, but returned for Michigan's conference title game win. The Wolverines then went on to win the College Football Playoff to cap a 15-0 season.

Harbaugh left for the Los Angeles Chargers after the season was over. In August of 2025, the NCAA formally punished the school, Harbaugh and others. Michigan was fined its postseason revenue sharing for the 2025 and 2026 seasons among myriad penalties, Harbaugh received a 10-year show-cause penalty and Stalions got an eight-year show-cause. Sherrone Moore, Harbaugh's successor and offensive coordinator for the 2023 team, was given an additional one-game suspension and a two-year show-cause.

The scandal : During the 2007 season, the New York Jets accused the New England Patriots of illegally filming their defensive signals during a game. The Patriots were later alleged to have been videotaping opposing coaches since Belichick was hired in 2000, a span of time including three Super Bowl titles. Belichick painted the matter as a differing interpretation of the rules — it wasn't specifically illegal to tape opposing coaches — but NFL commissioner Roger Goodell disagreed.

The penalty : The NFL fined Belichick $500,000, the Patriots $250,000 and stripped the team of its first-round pick in the 2008 NFL Draft.

The scandal : We're back on the Patriots, who blew out the Indianapolis Colts in the 2014 AFC championship game before winning Super Bowl XLIX. During that game, the Colts flagged that a ball intercepted from Tom Brady was noticeably deflated. An NFL investigation ensued and ultimately determined the Patriots had deliberately deflated balls at Brady's request. Nearly every development of this scandal was vociferously challenged by the Patriots.

The penalty : The NFL fined the Patriots $1 million and docked them their first-round pick in the 2016 NFL Draft and their fourth-round pick in the 2017 NFL Draft. It also suspended Brady four games without pay to open the 2015 season, which Brady had struck down in court only for it to be reinstated for the 2016 season.

The scandal : St. Louis Cardinals director of scouting Chris Correa was caught hacking the internal database of the Astros, using the accounts of former co-workers who helped build that database after leaving St. Louis for Houston. Correa, who was found to have acted alone, claimed he did it because he suspected the Astros of hacking the Cardinals.

The penalty : MLB ordered the Cardinals to pay $2 million to the Astros, as well as surrender their two highest picks in the 2017 MLB Draft to them. Correa was banned from baseball and sentenced to 46 months in prison after pleading guilty to five counts of unauthorized access of a protected computer.

The scandal : The Dolphins dreamed of pairing Brady with head coach Sean Payton. Unfortunately, both men were respectively under contract with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and New Orleans Saints. They were eventually found to have had impermissible contract with Brady and his agent Don Yee, who also represents Payton.

The penalty : The NFL docked the Dolphins a 2023 first-round pick and 2024 third-round pick, hit team owner Stephen Ross with a $1.5 million fine and six-game suspension and hit vice chairman Bruce Beal with $500,000 fine and year-long suspension.

The scandal : In late 2010, Buckeyes Mike Adams, Boom Herron, Devier Posey, Terrelle Pryor and Solomon Thomas were accused of receiving improper benefits from a Columbus tattoo parlor and suspended for the first five games of the 2011 season. As the owner of the tattoo parlor was under investigation for felony drug trafficking, Ohio State players were mentioned by the Department of Justice as trading memorabilia for tattoos or cash. Then-Ohio State coach Jim Tressel was given a heads up about the investigation via a confidential tip, and did not notify anyone else at Ohio State.

The penalty: Months after Tressel's emails became public and he said that he was trying to protect his players, he was suspended for two games and fined by Ohio State. The NCAA then accused him of potentially committing major violations.

In May of 2011, Tressel resigned as Ohio State's coach. In July, the NCAA vacated all of Ohio State's wins from the 2010 season and gave the Buckeyes a postseason ban for the 2012 season. Pryor, who was set to be a senior in 2011, instead declared for the NFL Draft. Current Wisconsin coach Luke Fickell served as Ohio State's interim coach in 2011 as the Buckeyes went 6-7. Ohio State hired Urban Meyer for the 2012 season after he spent 2011 as a TV analyst. Ohio State went undefeated in Meyer's first season and finished at No. 3 in the AP poll.

The scandal : After Reggie Bush won the 2005 Heisman Trophy at USC and was the No. 3 pick in the 2006 NFL Draft, Yahoo Sports reported after an eight-month investigation that Bush and his family had accepted benefits worth more than $100,000 from agents. Remember, the NCAA's amateurism rules were far different in 2005. A previous Yahoo Sports report about Bush's family's living arrangements led to the start of an NCAA investigation in April.

In the years after the Bush investigation began, the NCAA also began an investigation into benefits given to basketball player O.J. Mayo. The two investigations then became an all-encompassing one into USC's athletic department.

The penalty : USC, which won the BCS title at the end of the 2004 season, vacated the final two games of that season and every win it had in 2005. That BCS title was officially stripped in 2011. The program also received a two-year bowl ban in 2010 and 2011 along with significant scholarship reductions, as the NCAA's investigation took years to complete.

Bush also gave up his Heisman Trophy and the award for the 2005 season had been vacant for years. In 2024, the NCAA returned the trophy to Bush and reinstated him as the winner. Four years earlier, USC announced that it had ended its disassociation with Bush.

The scandal : There are no other doping cases on this list because those are largely treated as individual offenses. Russia is included because that really was a country's sporting arm engaging in rampant, state-sponsored doping for years and going to astonishing lengths to hide it from the authorities.

The penalty : In addition to dozens of athletes banned and medals stripped, the Russian flag has not been a common sight at the Olympics for years, due to both the doping scandal and its invasion of Ukraine.

The World Anti-Doping Agency hit the country with a four-year ban from international sports in 2019, while allowing individually cleared athletes to compete under a neutral banner. Russia appealed the decision with the Court of Arbitration for Sport, which both halved the ban to two years and further weakened some of the penalties.
